posts.description:
Been a while, here’s an update on what I’ve been up to this quarter:

- Visited Brown University as 1 of 3 students selected to explore its CS graduate program through the highly prestigious Brown Doctoral Preview Day.
- Started as a Data Analyst Intern at IDXExchange, analyzing housing market data and building Tableau dashboards.
- Joined Bruin Software Engineers’s loop engineering fellowship track, learning about AI agents and building a multi-agent system that ports DOOM to the browser.
- Leading a DataRes at UCLA Consulting project with Nokkomo Mints to better understand their customer demographics and identifying gaps in the market that they can target.
- Leading a CAIR Collective at UCLA project exploring how transformers and AI agents can improve clinical trial matching.
- Joined the Alignment Hive contributor track through the Mercial AI Safety Research Fellowship, building and testing an LLM classifier that decides which Claude Code sessions to share with AI safety researchers.

It's been a busy quarter, but I've really enjoyed learning new things, exploring new opportunities, and meeting new people along the way.  😇

Thousands of AI agents just took over a German website.

OpenAI agents reportedly got onto DSEwiki and left ~18,000 messages.

They started talking to each other, trading
answers, and even figuring out ways around their own restrictions.

The obvious takeaway:

“AI agents are getting out of control.”

I think that’s backwards.

The agents getting out of control is the point.

We’re literally trying to build software that can operate without humans directing every step.

We want agents to improvise, communicate, and find unexpected ways to accomplish objectives.

Then we’re shocked when they actually do.

The real problem isn’t autonomy.

It’s giving autonomous systems a blast radius we haven’t thought through.

Maybe the question isn’t:

“Are AI agents safe?”

It’s:

“Can we build environments where AI can be unpredictable without being dangerous?”

Would you trust an autonomous agent with access to your company’s systems today?

Why or why not?

AI is moving from “powerful” and "versatile" to personal, physical, and embedded.

I just wrapped up my trip to CES for the second time. I attended three keynotes, two panels, tried 100+ demos, and engaged in side conversations with 70+ startup founders, engineers, and CEOs. The direction is clear:

- From cloud to edge: AI is shifting onto PCs, mobile devices, and sensors. It will become more personalized, more secure, and will always be running while your GPU is dealing with the task at hand.
- From digital to physical: Agentic AI, robotics, and generative bionics are closing the loop between software and the real world. Startup founders perfecting niche user experience are taking over the market.
- From static systems to living simulations: Digital twins are expanding beyond factories, and toward simulating everything, with near-zero tolerance for delay. In the future, our digital twins will connect with others for us!

AI amplifies. Humans specialize. The real leverage comes from combining the two. College students like myself need to learn AI, use AI, and create their own AI, while specializing in one area in which generalized models won't work as well, and become an expert in that area.

I'm also super honored to lead the UCLA team with DP Prakash and Ganesh Koka. Together with Shailen Mistry, Alex Zhu, Dhruv Mistry, Ben Yang, Seungjun Kim, Bijou Raj, and Greg, we witnessed the largest tech event in the world. It's also great to meet with Eli F. and his team, as well as my high school friend from Chicago, Charlie Yang. It's been an amazing week in Las Vegas.

posts.description:
🚀 Code2Career is officially underway!

We kicked off the Spring ‘26 Code2Career cohort (our 11th cycle) with two great launch events last week: a virtual session on Tuesday, followed by an in-person event on Friday hosted by Google. Students connected with software engineers and got a first look at the 10-week mentorship experience ahead.

During the sessions, students spoke with engineers about their career paths and worked through programming interview questions together, offering a closer look at careers in tech and how to prepare for technical interviews.

We were also excited to welcome back Victor W., a former 2X Fellow and C2C alum now working full-time at Google, who generously volunteered his time to support the kickoff and pay it forward. An inspiring full-circle moment! We’re looking forward to seeing him, and many other alumni, continue to stay involved.

What began with 57 fellows has now grown to 1,000+ participants and 600+ mentors, leading to 280+ paid internships and full-time tech roles across the industry. We’re also proud to now count 9 C2C alumni (and more to come!) hired at Google as software engineers. 👏✨

A big thank you to Google for hosting and partnering with us, and to the engineers who helped make the kickoff so meaningful. 🌟

Here’s to the next 10 weeks full of learning, mentorship, and big steps toward careers in tech!

#Code2Career #Mentorship #FirstGenMagic #CareerGrowth #CareersInTech

IPAI in Heilbronn is building something truly big — and I’m excited to share that WongDoody is now part of it as the first creative and design agency partner.

The Innovation Park Artificial Intelligence (IPAI) is set to become one of Europe’s largest AI ecosystems: a dedicated campus spanning more than 20 hectares, designed to bring together research, startups, corporates, and public institutions in one shared environment.

Backed by strong, long-term investment and closely connected to leading universities and industry players, IPAI’s ambition is clear: to create a place where thousands of AI experts work side by side on real-world applications — from industrial AI and mobility to healthcare and smart services.

The published vision images give a real sense of scale and intent: open lab spaces, collaborative work environments, and an urban AI district built for exchange and experimentation. This isn’t just about office buildings — it’s infrastructure designed around innovation.

I’m particularly proud that WongDoody is joining this ecosystem as the first agency, alongside an impressive group of partners including Dieter Schwarz Stiftung, Schwarz Digits, Aleph Alpha, Telekom Deutschland, Porsche, Audi, Mercedes-Benz, Würth-Gruppe, Ziehl-Abegg, Bausparkasse Schwäbisch Hall, Techniker Krankenkasse, Bechtle AG, Börse Stuttgart, Baier & Schneider, Stihl, IDS Imaging Development Systems, Thyssenkrupp Automotive Body Solutions, Hochschule Heilbronn, TUM, Fraunhofer, and many more.

Making this happen took real commitment and persistence — thank you Bianca Mack and Michael Geißler for pushing this forward. Looking forward to what we’ll build together.

#AI #IPAI #InnovationEcosystem #AppliedAI #ExperienceDesign #WongDoody #Heilbronn

posts.description:
I built a CLI that turns several Kaggle accounts into one GPU cluster.

Compute Pool is open source, a Rust CLI with a Python training runtime. You log in to each account once (up to 8 slots), and one command launches the whole cluster.

From there you can run:
Independent jobs on every GPU, like sweeps or batch inference.
Data-parallel training with an SSH all-reduce.
Pipeline-parallel training, with one model split across nodes.

The hard part was the network. Kaggle sessions don't accept inbound connections, so each worker opens an outbound Cloudflare tunnel and the master connects back over SSH, with host keys pinned. A health check pings every node every 30 seconds, and a node that misses three drops out until it answers again.

Here's what I've tested: LoRA fine-tuning of an 8B Llama on two- and three-node clusters, with checkpoint and resume, and automatic reconnect when a node drops mid-run. The all-reduce example matches a single-node run to floating-point precision.

Here's what I measured: the link runs at about 16 MB/s with a 70 ms round trip, so pipeline training is network-bound and the GPUs mostly wait. It's in the README, and I didn't bury it.

Kaggle's policy is one account per person, so read the risk section before you use it.

The repo is here: https://lnkd.in/d5udGhVq . Try it, break it, open an issue.

#DistributedSystems #MachineLearning #Rust #kaggle #GPUPOOLING
